CHAPTER XLV.

NOT ALL A DREAM.

    “Where are the sounds that swam along
    The buoyant air when I was young;
    The last vibration now is o’er,
    And they who listened are no more;
    Ah! let me close my eyes and dream.”
              W. S. LANDOR.


The idea of Helstone had been suggested to Mr. Bell’s waking mind by his
conversation with Mr. Lennox, and all night long it ran riot through his
dreams. He was again the tutor in the college where he now held the rank
of Fellow; it was again a long vacation, and he was staying with his
newly-married friend, the proud husband, and happy Vicar of Helstone.
Over babbling brooks they took impossible leaps, which seemed to keep
them whole days suspended in the air. Time and space were not, though
all other things seemed real. Every event was measured by the emotions
of the mind, not by its actual existence, for existence it had none. But
the trees were gorgeous in their autumnal leafiness—the warm odours of
flower and herb came sweet upon the sense—the young wife moved about
the house with just that mixture of annoyance at her position, as
regarded wealth, with pride in her handsome and devoted husband, which
Mr. Bell had noticed in real life a quarter of a century ago. The dream
was so like life that, when he awoke, his present life seemed a dream.
Where was he? In the close, handsomely furnished room of a London hotel!
Where were those who spoke to him, moved around him, touched him, not an
instant ago? Dead! buried! lost for evermore, as far as earth’s for
evermore would extend. He was an old man, so lately exultant in the full
strength of manhood. The utter loneliness of his life was insupportable
to think about. He got up hastily, and tried to forget what never more
might be, in a hurried dressing for the breakfast in Harley Street.

He could not attend to all the lawyer’s details, which, as he saw, made
Margaret’s eyes dilate, and her lips grow pale, as one by one fate
decreed, or so it seemed, every morsel of evidence which would exonerate
Frederick, should fall from beneath her feet and disappear. Even Mr.
Lennox’s well-regulated professional voice took a softer, tenderer tone,
as he drew near to the extinction of the last hope. It was not that
Margaret had not been perfectly aware of the result before. It was only
that the details of each successive disappointment came with such
relentless minuteness to quench all hope, that she at last fairly gave
way to tears. Mr. Lennox stopped reading.

“I had better not go on,” said he, in a concerned voice. “It was a
foolish proposal of mine. Lieutenant Hale,” and even this giving him the
title of the service from which he had so harshly been expelled, was
soothing to Margaret. “Lieutenant Hale is happy now; more secure in
fortune and future prospects than he could ever have been in the navy;
and has, doubtless, adopted his wife’s country as his own.”

“That is it,” said Margaret. “It seems so selfish in me to regret it,”
trying to smile, “and yet he is lost to me, and I am so lonely.” Mr.
Lennox turned over his papers, and wished that he were as rich and
prosperous as he believed he should be some day. Mr. Bell blew his nose,
but, otherwise, he also kept silence; and Margaret, in a minute or two,
had apparently recovered her usual composure. She thanked Mr. Lennox
very courteously for his trouble; all the more courteously and
graciously because she was conscious that, by her behaviour, he might
probably be led to imagine that he had given her needless pain. Yet it
was pain she would not have been without.

Mr. Bell came up to wish her good-bye.

“Margaret!” said he, as he fumbled with his gloves, “I am going down to
Helstone to-morrow, to look at the old place. Would you like to come
with me? Or would it give you too much pain? Speak out, don’t be
afraid.”

“Oh, Mr. Bell,” said she—and could say no more. But she took his old
gouty hand, and kissed it.

“Come, come; that’s enough,” said he, reddening with awkwardness. “I
suppose your aunt Shaw will trust you with me. We’ll go to-morrow
morning, and we shall get there about two o’clock, I fancy. We’ll take a
snack, and order dinner at the little inn—the Lennard Arms, it used to
be—and go and get an appetite in the forest. Can you stand it,
Margaret? It will be a trial, I know, to both of us, but it will be a
pleasure to me, at least. And there we’ll dine—it will be but
doe-venison, if we can get it at all—and then I’ll take my nap, while
you go out and see old friends. I’ll give you back safe and sound,
barring railway accidents, and I’ll insure your life for a thousand
pounds before starting, which may be some comfort to your relations; but
otherwise, I’ll bring you back to Mrs. Shaw by lunch time on Friday. So,
if you say yes, I’ll just go upstairs and propose it.”

“It’s no use my trying to say how much I shall like it,” said Margaret,
through her tears.

“Well, then, prove your gratitude by keeping those fountains of yours
dry for the next two days. If you don’t, I shall feel queer myself about
the lachrymal ducts, and I don’t like that.”

“I won’t cry a drop,” said Margaret, winking her eyes to shake the tears
off her eyelashes, and forcing a smile.

“There’s my good girl. Then we’ll go upstairs and settle it all.”
Margaret was in a state of almost trembling eagerness, while Mr. Bell
discussed his plan with her aunt Shaw, who was first startled, then
doubtful and perplexed, and in the end, yielding rather to the rough
force of Mr. Bell’s words than to her own conviction; for to the last,
whether it was right or wrong, proper or improper, she could not settle
to her own satisfaction, till Margaret’s safe return, the happy
fulfilment of the project, gave her decision enough to say, “she was
sure it had been a very kind thought of Mr. Bell’s, and just what she
herself had been wishing for Margaret, as giving her the very change
which she required, after all the anxious time she had had.”

He was young again, not a respected college Fellow but a lowly tutor, lingering through the long vacation as the guest of his newly married, giddy friend: the proud, overjoyed new Vicar of Helstone, Richard Hale. The two of them bounded across babbling little brooks in wild, impossible leaps, that hung suspended mid-air for what felt like whole sunlit days. Time and space melted away, even as every other detail felt sharp and true. No event followed the rules of real life, measured not by clock or calendar but by the soft swell of shared emotion, for none of it was real — and yet it all felt more vivid than his waking hours. The beech trees blazed in rich autumn crimson, the warm scents of wild herb and late blooming rose drifted thick and sweet on the breeze, and the young Mrs. Hale moved through the little parsonage with that exact familiar mixture of faint, playful irritation at their narrow household means, and unashamed pride in her handsome, adoring husband, that Bell had observed in real life a full quarter of a century prior.

The dream was so lifelike that when he jolted awake, his whole present life felt like the false, hollow fantasy. Where was he? Stuck in the close, over-furnished, stuffy rooms of a central London hotel! Where were the friends who had been laughing, speaking, brushing his sleeve not a heartbeat before? Dead. Buried. Lost forever, as far as any mortal “forever” could stretch. He was an old man now, his joints aching, even though only moments ago in the dream he had been brimming with the untested strength of youth. The utter, crushing loneliness of his life was too much to bear for a single second longer sitting still, so he stumbled out of bed and dressed at a rushed, clumsy pace, desperate to outrun the ghosts of the past and make it to the breakfast appointment in Harley Street.

He could barely focus on the fine details of Lennox’s legal presentation, even as he watched Margaret’s eyes grow wide and bright with tension, her lips blanching one by one, as every last scrap of evidence that might have exonerated Frederick Hale crumbled out from under them, one after another, as if fate itself had decreed no such proof could remain. Even Mr. Lennox, whose professional tone was always so measured and unshakable, softened into a gentle, tender cadence as he drew close to laying the last of their hopes to rest. It was not that Margaret had not known this outcome was likely all along: it was the relentless, sharp minuteness of every successive disappointment, laid bare one after another, that finally wore down her resolve, and she gave way to quiet, shaking tears.

Mr. Lennox set his papers down at once. “I ought not to go on with this,” he said, his voice thick with concern. “This was a foolish, ill-advised proposal of mine. Lieutenant Hale —” he used the naval title he had been so harshly stripped of, a small, soft gesture of respect that soothed Margaret more than any other comfort could — “is happy now. His fortune and his future across the sea are far more secure than anything he ever could have hoped for in the Royal Navy, and no doubt he has long since adopted his wife’s homeland as his own.”

“That is all true,” Margaret managed, trying to force a wobbly smile through her tears. “I feel so selfish for grieving as I do. But he is lost to me, and I am so very lonely.”

Mr. Lennox shuffled his papers into a neat stack, and silently wished with all his might that he was already as wealthy and successful as he was certain he would be in the years to come, so he could wave away every last one of her troubles. Mr. Bell blew his nose loudly into his handkerchief, and otherwise kept quiet, giving her space to collect herself. In a minute or two, Margaret had regained her usual quiet composure, and thanked Mr. Lennox with a courtesy and grace that was almost exaggerated, for she was all too aware that her tears might have led him to believe he had inflicted unnecessary pain. And yet, for all the sharp ache it carried, she would not have missed that full, honest reckoning with her loss for anything.

Mr. Bell shuffled over to her to say his goodbyes, his fumbling gout-ridden fingers tangling in his thick leather gloves. “Margaret,” he said, “I’m heading down to Helstone tomorrow, to go look over the old place. Would you like to come with me? Or would it be far too painful? Speak plain, don’t mince words on my account.”

“Oh, Mr. Bell —” Margaret could not get any more words past her tight throat. She only lifted his gnarled, swollen old hand and pressed a soft kiss to it.

“Come now, that’s quite enough of that,” he grumbled, his face flushing bright pink with awkward pleasure. “I’m sure your aunt Shaw will trust you in my care. We’ll leave first thing tomorrow morning, get there around two o’clock, I reckon. We’ll grab a light snack, order dinner at the little inn — the Lennard Arms, that’s what it used to be called — and then go wander the forest to work up an appetite. Can you bear it, Margaret? It’ll be a trial for both of us, I know, but it’ll be a pleasure to me, at the very least. We’ll dine there on roast venison, if the innkeeper still has access to the forest deer, and then I’ll take my usual afternoon nap while you go out and call on any remaining old friends from the parsonage days. I’ll bring you back safe and sound, barring railway accidents, and I’ll insure your life for a thousand pounds before we start out, that ought to be some comfort to your relations. I’ll have you back with Mrs. Shaw by lunchtime on Friday, no later. So if you say yes, I’ll go straight upstairs and put the plan to her.”

“There’s no way I can possibly tell you how much I want to go,” Margaret said, the tears still dripping down her cheeks.

“Alright then, prove your gratitude by drying those tear ducts up for the next two days,” Bell ordered gruffly. “If you don’t, I’ll get all wobbly lipped myself, and I hate that more than anything.”

“I won’t shed a single more drop,” Margaret promised, winking hard to shake the leftover tears off her eyelashes and forcing a bright, steady smile.

“That’s my good girl. Now let’s go upstairs and sort all of this out.”

Margaret was trembling with quiet, eager hope as Mr. Bell laid out his plan to Aunt Shaw, who went through every predictable stage of reaction: first startled, then doubtful, then hopelessly perplexed over whether the excursion was at all proper for a young unmarried woman. In the end she yielded far more to Mr. Bell’s gruff, earnest good sense than to her own uncertain misgivings, for right up until the day Margaret returned safe and sound, she could not make up her own mind if the trip was right or wrong, appropriate or unseemly. By the time the pair stepped back through the Harley Street door, the project had proved such a glowing success that Aunt Shaw declared without hesitation that it had been the kindest, most thoughtful idea Mr. Bell could possibly have had, and exactly the rest Margaret needed after all the long, anxious months of trouble she had weathered.
